primary_sources: Angelina Grimké, Appeal to the Christian Women of the South, 1836

stimulus.text:
Angelina Grimké, Appeal to the Christian Women of the South (1836):

“But perhaps you will be ready to query, why appeal to women on this subject? We do not make the laws which perpetuate slavery. No legislative power is vested in us; we can do nothing to overthrow the system, even if we wished to do so. To this I reply, I know you do not make the laws, but I also know that you are the wives and mothers, the sisters and daughters of those who do; and if you really suppose you can do nothing to overthrow slavery, you are greatly mistaken. You can do much in every way: four things I will name. 1st. You can read on this subject. 2d. You can pray over this subject. 3d. You can speak on this subject. 4th. You can act on this subject.”

Grimké added that laws forbidding Southerners to free enslaved people or teach them to read, “such wicked laws ought to be no barrier in the way of your duty.”

Background: Grimké was born into a slaveholding family in Charleston, South Carolina, and had moved north to join the abolitionist cause.
stimulus.source_note: Quotations verbatim from Angelina Grimké, Appeal to the Christian Women of the South, The Anti-Slavery Examiner, September 1836, public domain, as printed on Wikisource.

stem: Grimké's appeal best illustrates which chain of causes in Period 4?

options.text: The Awakening's belief in perfecting society led converts into abolition
The cotton gin made slavery unprofitable, so Southerners welcomed abolition
options.misconception: The cotton gin made slavery more profitable, not less.

options.text: Congress had already banned slavery, and Grimké was celebrating the fact
options.misconception: Slavery was legal and growing in 1836; Congress had banned nothing of the kind.

options.text: The market revolution ended all reform movements by 1836
options.misconception: Reform was growing in the 1830s, not ending.

rationales.A: Revival preaching taught that people could perfect themselves and then perfect society. Grimké carries that belief straight into abolition.
rationales.B: The gin cleaned cotton fast, so planters grew more of it. Slavery grew with the gin, it did not fade.
rationales.C: Congress banned only the importation of enslaved people, in 1808. Slavery itself stayed legal and grew.
rationales.D: The 1830s were the great decade of reform: temperance, abolition, schools, and women's rights all grew.
rationales.general:
1. Start with the revival. The Second Great Awakening taught that converts could perfect themselves and then perfect society.
2. Follow the belief. Grimké, raised in a slaveholding family, turned that belief against slavery itself.
3. Name the chain. Revival made reformers, and reformers made abolitionists.
Background: William Lloyd Garrison's Liberator, begun in 1831, demanded immediate emancipation.
Remember: to trace a movement, follow one belief from the pulpit to the petition.
